initial_prompt: Explain quantum entanglement to a 12-year-old in about 3 short paragraphs.

messages.content: Explain quantum entanglement to a 12-year-old in about 3 short paragraphs.

Imagine you have two magic coins that are made together in a special way. When you flip them, each coin can land on heads or tails, but here’s the weird part: until you actually look, it’s like each coin is in a “both at once” fuzzy state. Now, if these two magic coins are *entangled*, the moment you look at one and see it’s heads, the other one instantly “decides” what it must be—no matter how far away it is.

In real life, instead of coins, scientists use tiny particles, like electrons or photons (little bits of light). When particles are entangled, they share a kind of hidden connection. If you measure one particle and find out something about it (like which way it’s spinning), you immediately know what the result for the other particle must be, even if it’s on the other side of the Earth.

What makes this so strange is that nothing seems to travel between them—this change appears to happen faster than light could go. Even famous scientists like Einstein thought this was “spooky.” But experiments show it really happens. We don’t think the particles are “talking” to each other; instead, quantum physics says their properties were never separate to begin with—they’re like two parts of the same “question,” and you only see the full answer when you measure them.
